passage: Rohan visited a shop to buy a new cricket bat marked at ₹2,000. The shopkeeper offered a 10% discount on the marked price. To find the discount amount, we calculate 10% of ₹2,000, which is ₹200. Thus, the selling price becomes ₹1,800. Rohan decided to sell his old bat for ₹500, which he had originally bought for ₹400. Since the selling price is higher than the cost price, he made a profit of ₹100. He calculated his profit percentage by dividing the profit by the cost price, resulting in 25%. Later, Rohan invested ₹1,000 in a bank at a simple interest rate of 10% per annum for 6 months. To calculate the interest, he converted 6 months into 0.5 years. Using the formula (Principal × Rate × Time) / 100, he found the interest to be ₹50. Finally, he considered a scheme offering two successive discounts of 10% and 20%. He correctly calculated that this is not a flat 30% discount, because the second discount is applied only to the already reduced price. By applying these methods, Rohan avoided common mistakes and managed his finances effectively.

items.evidence: He calculated his profit percentage by dividing the profit by the cost price, resulting in 25%.
items.q: Rohan sold his old bat for ₹500. How did he get 25% as his profit percent?
options: He divided ₹100 by the ₹400 cost price
He divided ₹100 by the ₹500 selling price
He divided ₹500 by the ₹400 cost price
He divided ₹100 by the ₹2,000 marked price
items.explain: Profit percent uses the cost price: ₹100 ÷ ₹400 × 100 = 25%.

wrong.why: thinks profit percent is found on the selling price
treats the selling price as the profit
picks a nearby number from the passage

items.evidence: He correctly calculated that this is not a flat 30% discount, because the second discount is applied only to the already reduced price.
items.q: Why do successive discounts of 10% and 20% not make a flat 30% discount?
options: The 20% is taken from the already lowered price
The 20% is taken from the original marked price
The 10% is taken from the price after 20%
The 20% is added back to the lowered price
items.explain: The second discount, 20%, applies only to the price already reduced by 10%.

wrong.why: thinks both percents come from the same base
reverses the order of the two discounts
thinks percent changes cancel each other out

items.evidence: To find the discount amount, we calculate 10% of ₹2,000, which is ₹200.
items.q: If the bat were marked ₹3,000 with the same 10% discount, what would the discount be?
items.explain: The discount is 10% of the marked price, and 10% of ₹3,000 is ₹300.

wrong.why: thinks 10% is always the same amount
mixes up the discount with the selling price

items.evidence: To calculate the interest, he converted 6 months into 0.5 years.
items.q: Rohan put ₹1,000 in a bank at 10% per annum for 6 months. Why is his interest ₹50?
options: The time is half a year, not one year
The rate drops to 5% for six months
The bank keeps ₹50 back as a fee
items.explain: The rate is per year, so 6 months is 0.5 years: 1000 × 10 × 0.5 ÷ 100 = ₹50.

wrong.why: halves the rate instead of the time
halves the principal instead of the time
guesses from everyday banking instead of using the formula
